item.title: Exploring Mapping Malcolm with Najha Zigbi-Johnson — Sat Aug 29, 12:00 PM — Nasher Museum of Art
item.description:
Join author and scholar Najha Zigbi-Johnson for a gallery talk exploring Mapping Malcolm in conversation with the exhibition, Turn the volume up! Moderated by Durham-based artist Marcella Zigbuo Camara, the discussion will examine how artists, writers, and cultural thinkers engage questions of place, memory, identity, resistance, and collective liberation.
Visitors are invited to engage with the exhibition through the lens of Mapping Malcolm, discovering unexpected connections between contemporary artistic practice and the enduring legacy of Malcolm X.

item.description: Stories for a Saturday Night: An Evening with Ira Glass This American Life host Ira Glass brings a night of storytelling in the style he pioneered on his hit radio show: funny stories with feelings. His program is heard each week by over three million listeners and has won the highest honors in broadcasting, including three Emmys (for a TV adaptation), eight Peabody Awards and the first Pulitzer Prize ever given to a radio show or podcast. For decades, it’s been one of the most popular podcasts in the world. Glass invented a way to tell radio stories that reshaped audio storytelling and has been widely imitated. item.title: NCJSS Welcomes Saskia Ziolkowski — Sun Aug 30, 3:00 PM — John Hope Franklin Center 230-232
item.description:
The North Carolina Jewish Studies Seminar welcomes Saskia Ziolkowski, Associate Professor of Romance Studies at Duke University. Ziolkowski works on Italian literature and culture from a comparative perspective, especially in terms of the connections between Italy and German-language countries. Her research topics include modernism, the novel, animal studies, world literature, Jewish studies, migration, literary history, and issues of identity. Her book Kafka's Italian Progeny (University of Toronto Press, awarded the American Association of Italian Studies 2020 Book Prize in Literary Studies) explores Franz Kafka's sometimes surprising connections with key writers - from Massimo Bontempelli, Lalla Romano, and Italo Calvino to Antonio Tabucchi, Paola Capriolo, and Elena Ferrante - who have shaped Italy's literary landscape.

item.title: CEE Seminar - Towards Nature-Based Solutions for Rivers and Coastal Zones Characterizing the Role of Vegetation — Mon Aug 31, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: Aquatic vegetation provides a range of essential ecosystem services in rivers and coastal zones. By reducing near-bed flow, vegetation provides habitat, reduces sediment suspension, and stabilizes river channels. By damping waves and storm surges, coastal wetlands offer shoreline protection. These ecosystem services are mediated by the physical interaction between flowing water and plants. This talk presents results from theoretical and experimental studies that characterize flow-vegetation interactions across a range of spatial scales and flow conditions. It is shown that the drag generated by individual plants is predicted by a fundamental force balance involving plant stiffness, plant buoyancy, and hydrodynamic forcing. This plant-scale drag is also linked to canopy-scale hydrodynamics, with implications for river restoration and coastal protection. item.title: DMI/MEMS Seminar Presented by Prof Quinn Besford — Mon Aug 31, 12:00 PM — Teer 203
item.description: Abstract: Spatially resolving stimuli can allow us to better understand physicochemical processes in complex environments [1,2]. Towards this goal, we develop ways of integrating Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) chemistry into stimuli-responsive polymer architectures, such that FRET output (i.e., spectral shift in fluorescence) reflects polymer chain conformation [3]. Using FRET, we can spatially resolve conformation by confocal microscopy methods, with high spatiotemporal resolution. In this talk, I will discuss strategies to integrate FRET into functional polymers, and how we can examine the responsiveness of the polymers for understanding physicochemical processes. Specifically, these systems are used to study surface wettability [3], localised changes in pH [1], resolving contact areas between surfaces, and micro-to-nano structure in secondary matrices [5]. item.title: PE/PI Workshop: David Fortunato (UCSD) — Mon Aug 31, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 230E
item.description:
David Fortunato (UCSD) will present, "Choosing Legislative Capacity: A Theoretical Model." (with Florian Hollenbach and Rosanne Logeart)
Abstract: In democracies, elected representatives in legislatures compete with unelected bureaucrats for influence over policy outcomes. A determining factor in this competition is the legislature's procedural organization and endowment of tangible resources for legislative work, both of which shape its overall capacity for policy design and oversight. Importantly, nearly every democratic legislature is empowered to choose its organizational rules and resource endowment, creating a fascinating strategic choice at the heart of each democratic system: how much capacity will the legislature grant itself? We present a theoretical model of this choice in light of the legislative majority's present and expected orientation toward the bureaucracy, its preferential dissimilarity from the opposition, and its expectations for deselection. item.title: Luminary & Freedom Stories — Fri Sep 18, 7:00 PM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.
Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.
---
Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"
Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. item.title: The 1868 North Carolina Constitution — Tue Sep 29, 5:00 PM — Wilson Library
item.description:
North Carolina’s 1868 Constitution rebuilt the state after the Civil War, expanding political participation and redefining the relationship between government and citizens in the state’s first attempt at multiracial democracy. This lecture examines how that document laid the groundwork for principles that continue to shape North Carolina constitutional law, and what its lessons offer for constitutional debates still unresolved 250 years after the state’s founding.
Speakers: Marcus Gadson, associate professor of law, and Harry L. Watson, Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture
About the Speakers:
Professor Marcus Gadson is an associate professor of law at UNC School of Law, joining the faculty in 2025. He teaches courses on State Constitutional Law, federal Constitutional Law, and civil procedure. item.title: Get Shit Done - SQSN — Tue Oct 20, 5:30 PM — 114 - living room
item.description:
This event is intended for Queer and/or Trans survivors:Some of the biggest barriers to survivor safety are finance related. While we do our best to put cash directly into survivors hands, in tandem, we thought it would be awesome to create a body doubling/coworking space where we can support each other in sifting through all the shit that goes into getting financial stable. And offer relevant financial resources as we find them!That’s why we host our “Get Shit Done” evenings. They will occur the 1st & 3rd Tuesday of each month and be available in person or online (must register or email advocate@lgbtqcenterofdurham.org for the virtual link). If you or someone you know is a money expert who wants to share their knowledge with queer/trans survivors, please reach out!

item.title: Mike Wiley: One Noble Journey — Fri Oct 23, 4:00 PM — Hill Hall
item.description:
FEATURING
Mike Wiley
Mike Wiley holds a Masters of Fine Arts from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and was the 2010 and 2014 Lehman Brady Visiting Joint Chair Professor in Documentary Studies and American Studies at Duke University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Wiley received the University of North Carolina’s Distinguished Alumni Award in 2017.
PROGRAM
One Noble Journey
Henry “Box” Brown was an African American born into slavery in 1816 in Louisa County, Virginia. Although he was not subjected to physical violence, Henry’s story (the basis for One Noble Journey) demonstrates the cruelty of slavery was every bit as devastating to the heart as it could be on the body.After his family was torn apart and parceled out to various beneficiaries of the estate, Henry devised an ingenious escape plan – sealing himself in a wooden box for shipment to friends and freedom in Philadelphia.
